one_liner: Single-header AES-NI 128-bit hash: about 4x XXH64 bulk throughput in SMHasher3, but fails 55/250 quality tests.
what_it_does: AquaHash is a 128-bit non-cryptographic hash for x86 CPUs with AES-NI. It ships as one 440-line C++ header (aquahash.h) holding a single class. The API differs from xxHash: AquaHash::Hash(const uint8_t*, size_t, __m128i seed = 0) returns an __m128i, and an incremental object provides Initialize/Update/Finalize. The two component algorithms (SmallKeyAlgorithm, LargeKeyAlgorithm) are public too, and VerifyImplementation() checks built-in test vectors.
how_it_is_fast: Each 16-byte input block becomes the round key of a single AES round (_mm_aesenc_si128), so the whole per-block cost is one AES instruction. Keys of 64 bytes or more are spread across four independent 128-bit lanes (a 512-bit block), which keeps the AES units pipelined; the lanes are mixed and reduced with a few AES rounds only at the end. Keys under 64 bytes take a single-lane path: the 1-15-byte tail is XORed in with constant-padded vectors and three AES rounds finish the hash, with no cross-lane reduction. The author's blog gives 15 bytes/cycle bulk on Skylake and about 25 cycles per hash at the smallest key sizes.
when_to_use: Non-adversarial bulk checksums, deduplication or content fingerprinting of large buffers on x86-64 with AES-NI, when bytes/cycle is the bottleneck (SMHasher3: 15.84 bytes/cycle vs 12.82 for XXH3-64 and 3.99 for XXH-64).
As a fast pre-filter where every hash match is confirmed by a byte comparison, so extra collisions cost time but never correctness.
Clang-built, x86-only codebases that want a tiny Apache-2.0 header with no dependencies to vendor and patch.
As a compact reference point when studying AES-round hash constructions next to Meow hash.
when_not_to_use: Hash tables, or any use that needs good distribution on structured keys. SMHasher3 finds full 128-bit collisions on the Sparse, Cyclic and Permutation keysets: for example, 405 collisions among 22.4M 64-byte keys with at most 3 bits set, where 0 are expected. An open 2019 issue (#7) reports 3,488,136 collisions in a brute-force test that should give about 312.
Short keys: its 34.31 cycles average on 1-32 bytes is slower than wyhash (29.31), XXH3-64 (30.69) and a5hash (26.91) in the same SMHasher3 table.
Untrusted input or HashDoS defence: the author says it is not suitable for cryptographic use, and it fails SMHasher3's Seed, SeedSparse and SeedBlockLen tests.
ARM or any CPU without AES-NI: the code calls x86 intrinsics directly and has no fallback path.

Anything that needs a maintained dependency or an unpatched GCC build: the upstream header does not compile with GCC (issue #1, open since 2019), issues are now disabled, and there have been no commits since 2019-03-06.

integration.dependencies: None beyond the x86 intrinsic headers <smmintrin.h> and <wmmintrin.h>.
integration.min_toolchain: Not documented. The features used (constexpr, brace-initialised member arrays) need C++11, and the author says the code came from a C++17 codebase. The author says it compiles cleanly with Clang in strict mode. Upstream fails on GCC (reported on 4.9 and 8.2.1) because LargeKeyAlgorithm declares `__m128 block[4]` where `__m128i` is needed. AES codegen must be enabled (-maes or a suitable -march). MSVC is not documented.
integration.platforms: x86/x86-64 with AES-NI only. There is no ARM or portable fallback.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The static Hash/SmallKeyAlgorithm/LargeKeyAlgorithm functions keep no shared state (read from source). An incremental AquaHash object is unsynchronised.

gotchas: The result is a by-value __m128i. Writing it through a cast pointer into an unaligned buffer can crash: issue #3 reports SMHasher's BulkSpeed test segfaulting this way. Store it with _mm_storeu_si128.
Upstream has no std::hash-style adapter and no 64-bit output. For hash tables you must pull 64 bits out of the __m128i yourself (the hungptit fork adds such a wrapper).
After Finalize() the incremental object is in an undefined state and must be re-Initialize()d. Only an assert guards against double finalization, so release builds get no check.

Hash() switches from the small-key to the large-key algorithm at 64 bytes, and calling a component function directly outside its intended range gives values that differ from Hash(). Tail bytes are read through reinterpret_cast'ed uint64/32/16 pointers: these are unaligned, aliasing-violating loads that the author's x86 targets tolerate.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Meow hash or xxHash's XXH3 only when raw x86 bulk throughput on non-adversarial data matters more than hash quality: SMHasher3 puts AquaHash at 15.84 bytes/cycle against Meow's 12.43 and XXH3-64's 12.82, but Meow passes all 250 tests and XXH3 is portable and maintained. For short keys, wyhash and a5hash are both faster and better tested, so do not pick AquaHash there.
verified_claims_summary: SMHasher3's results summary (CPU and compiler not stated; GiB/s figures are converted at a nominal 3.5 GHz) measures AquaHash at 15.84 bytes/cycle bulk against 3.99 for XXH-64 (about 4x) and 12.82 for XXH3-64 (about 1.24x), and at 34.31 cycles average on 1-32-byte keys against 52.60 for XXH-64 and 29.31 for wyhash. The author's Skylake graph against xxhash64 and FarmHash gives no compiler or flags, and a 2019 third-party fork benchmark (clang 8) timed its aquahash command at 131.6 ms against 163.2 ms for xxhsum on a 100 MB+ file, about 1.24x including I/O.
status_note: Abandoned since the 2019-03-06 v1.0 commit: issues are disabled and the GCC-build and collision-rate reports were never answered with fixes. It is Apache-2.0 and one 440-line header, so it is easy to vendor and patch; the hungptit fork already fixes the GCC error.
